source.title: Corpora duplication for NLP in low-resource languages: A case study of Nahuatl
source.citation: Juan Jose Guzman Landa et al., 2026
source.authors: Juan Jose Guzman Landa; Juan-Manuel Torres-Moreno; Luis-Gil Moreno-Jiménez; Elvys Linhares Pontes; Miguel Figueroa-Saavedra; Graham Ranger; Martha Lorena Avendaño Garrido

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream semantic-similarity performance across corpus-duplication levels, conceptually testing whether downstream performance improves with scale. It uses static embeddings and Kendall’s tau rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own results for static embeddings trained on duplicated corpora and evaluated on semantic similarity. It does not measure held-out language-model loss, fit power laws, or test a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Cited scaling-law and deduplication findings are not this study’s results. Balancing-only comparisons and pretrained baseline scores do not test the scale-related version recorded here.
record.test_reason: The study trains static word embeddings (Word2Vec, FastText, GloVe) on a Nahuatl corpus duplicated up to 50 times. It scores them on one 30-item sentence-similarity task (Kendall's tau). It cites Kaplan et al. only as background. It fits no power law and measures no language-model loss, compute or parameter scaling. Its 'scale' axis is repetition of the same 6.6M-token corpus at fixed epochs, not unique data or model size. The systems are static embeddings, not the language models the versions name. V6 concerns language-model downstream performance improving predictably with scale or loss; predictability is never assessed here. V5 'repeated data' requires the power-law form, which is not tested. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version instead.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that duplication alone, without balancing, improves results. They find positional balancing beats uniform balancing. Uniform balancing plus duplication deteriorates tau from rho=2 in several cases. They propose rho=12 as a reasonably optimal duplication ratio and present duplication as an efficient way to expand corpora for low-resource languages.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses static word embeddings trained on a duplicated low-resource-language corpus and evaluates semantic similarity; it does not use neural-language-model cross-entropy scaling fits or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by embedding algorithm and architecture, balancing method, and duplication ratio. The authors report that topic positional balancing performs especially well, FastText and Word2Vec peak at different duplication levels, GloVe has diminishing results, and further duplication can plateau or reduce scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Repeating a 6.6M-token Nahuatl corpus raises static-embedding sentence-similarity tau up to a peak (FastText rho≈8–12, Word2Vec rho≈12–22). Scores then plateau or fall below the starting score by rho=50. With uniform balancing, duplication degrades tau from rho=2 in several cases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For static word embeddings in low-resource languages, moderate corpus repetition improves downstream semantic similarity, with an optimum and diminishing or negative returns at high repetition.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the Sixth Workshop on NLP for Indigenous Languages of the Americas (AmericasNLP)
record.problems: The evidence concerns static embeddings and one sentence-level semantic-similarity task, not language-model loss. Results are limited to Nahuatl and a small evaluation set of 30 reference sentences judged by 5 native speakers. The reported run variability is plotted as standard-deviation bands, without numerical uncertainty values in the cited results.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the tested version. Table 3 balancing-only results, pretrained baseline comparisons, and cited results from other work were excluded because they do not report the effect of corpus scale/duplication on the tested downstream-performance relation.

untested.parts: No held-out LM loss; no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count; CBOW vs skip-gram is an objective difference, not a depth/width difference.
Repeated data is studied, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.
No language-model downstream performance; no predictability of performance from scale or loss.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits to compare.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V6 supports and limits_scope labels is overturned. The subjects are static embeddings, not language models. The 'scale' axis is corpus repetition at fixed epochs, and no scaling law or predictability is assessed. Evaluation uses 30 reference sentences. Variability is shown only as standard-deviation bands.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.
The same power-law form in other modalities or training regimes; corpus duplication is studied, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.
The study evaluates one sentence-level semantic-similarity task with static embeddings; it does not test other downstream tasks or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.

relation.reason: Kaplan et al. is cited as introductory motivation; the experiments provide no power-law fit, language-model loss scaling, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates corpus balancing and duplication for static embeddings on sentence similarity. It neither tests a listed scaling-law version nor uses a fitted scaling law as a tool.

source_check.notes: The authors_conclusion paraphrase matches the text. R1–R7 contain selected maxima; all rows concern static embeddings and appropriately link to no claim version.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Unbalanced π-YALLI duplication for FastText and Word2Vec, and topic-positionally balanced duplication at ρ=12
reader_labels.reason: The reported best downstream semantic-similarity scores are higher than the unexpanded baselines for these settings (R1, R2, R6, R7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GloVe and high duplication levels in the topic-positionally balanced experiments
reader_labels.reason: GloVe’s gain is small, and at high duplication Word2Vec falls below its initial score while FastText stays near its initial baseline; the authors also report a limit to further improvement (R5, R8, R9).
